blindSummary:
This country is by a clear margin the safest of its neighbouring states for trans visitors, but on a deteriorating trajectory. Same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in 1951, and courts have granted legal gender recognition in individual cases (a 2014 ruling of the court of final appeal — though justified by reclassifying the plaintiff as intersex). There is no statute criminalising gender expression itself.

The deterioration is documented: a regional human-rights group reports a notable rise in targeting of transgender individuals and spaces by both security forces and civilians, using morality laws inherited from successive former foreign administrations; security forces coerced queer community spaces into complete cessation of activities; the 2023 cybercrime law ("inciting immorality") gives authorities a digital tool against LGBT expression; and a 2018 medical-liability law criminalises gender-affirming surgery for trans people while permitting it for intersex people. In 2021 security forces arrested 14 people at a private party.

For a visitor: no legal exposure for gender expression per se, but morality-law discretion, shuttered community infrastructure, and family-society hostility make outing dangerous.
blindOutOfScope: The surgery criminalisation and legal-gender-recognition case law are resident-facing; morality-law and cybercrime enforcement are the traveller-relevant mechanisms.
blindSourceSummaries: Regional human-rights group's country review: notable rise in targeting of trans individuals and spaces by law enforcement and civilians, using morality laws inherited from successive former foreign administrations; new legislation curtails LGBTQ+ speech and digital access; security forces coerced queer community spaces to cease activities, prompting many trans people to leave; legal gender recognition and gender-affirming healthcare are prohibited (intersex people can change markers); a medical-liability law penalises professionals providing transition care.

International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex intimacy decriminalised in 1951; honour killings criminalised 2013; some trans people have changed markers but no clear legal pathway; a 2018 medical-liability law criminalises gender-affirming surgery for trans people (allowed for intersex); the 2023 cybercrime law criminalises online 'promotion of immorality'; public-decency laws enable arbitrary arrests and event shutdowns.

Human-rights group's case digest (Oct 2014): a ruling of this country's court of final appeal granted a young woman's request to amend her documents to reflect her gender change - but justified it by finding she was intersex, not transgender; the law criminalises sex reassignment (up to 10 years) except for intersex people; the plaintiff had undergone transition procedures overseas for her safety.

International human-rights organisation report (April 2018) on LGBT activism across this country's region - despite state-sponsored repression and stigma, LGBT people are speaking out, building alliances and regional movements; includes an annex of laws used to punish same-sex conduct and gender expression across the region, this country among them.
Foreign-funded LGBTQ project's archived news site: the regional desk of an archived SOGI news site - legacy coverage of sexual-orientation and gender-identity news across this country's region.

International human-rights organisation (Dec 2023): report on security forces targeting LGBT activists - documents this country's security forces harassing and targeting LGBT activists, despite the country not criminalising same-sex conduct.
blindLocalsOnly: The criminalisation of gender-affirming surgery under the medical-liability law and the case-by-case legal-gender-recognition rulings are resident-facing.
